periods.analysis: We start this run with the gateway doing what a gateway is supposed to do: move commerce at scale, with containerized cargo at 1,205,354 TEUs, cruise passengers at 4,371,952 guests, and petroleum throughput at 133,333,565 barrels. All three demand measures are green, and that tells me the airport-seaport market is still choosing Harborview. The yellow flag is not demand; it is operating slack, with berth and terminal utilization at 81.8% against a ceiling of 80%. When Berths 7, 8, and the Southport container apron all run hot in the same tide cycle, one late ship can turn a strong quarter into a queue.
periods.recommendations: Hold the green volume by extending the Tuesday-Thursday night gate at Terminal 4 and keeping the Gate 14 OCR lanes fully staffed during the 0500-0900 import push. Put a weekly watch on berth conflicts above 80%, especially cruise-container overlaps on Fridays and Saturdays. I want the Harborview Port Ops desk to publish a 21-day berth heat map for carriers, pilots, fuel schedulers, and cruise lines so we protect the growth without pretending the cushion is larger than it is.

periods.analysis: The holiday and winter cruise season arrived hard: cruise passenger throughput rose by 965,128 to 5,337,080 guests, while containerized cargo eased by 23,657 to 1,181,697 TEUs and stayed green. Berth and terminal utilization moved the wrong way, up 2.8 percentage points to 84.6%, which is why I am still calling this a yellow operating quarter. Petroleum throughput slipped by 3,763,449 to 129,570,116 barrels, just under the 130,000,000 target, and that puts fuel scheduling on the watch board with berths. The port is commercially strong, but Q4 showed us that cruise peaks, container cutoffs, and tanker windows are now competing for the same scarce hours.
periods.recommendations: Keep the cruise gains by extending the Terminal 2 and Terminal 18 baggage hall staffing model that cleared the Oasis-class turn days before 1130. For the yellow items, reserve two protected tanker windows per week at the petroleum dock and require 72-hour confirmation from the top five fuel shippers. Start a berth-rebalancing pilot with the harbor pilots and SSA yard team so utilization moves back toward 80% without sacrificing the green TEU and guest base.

periods.analysis: Q1 was the quarter where the margin got too thin for my taste: containerized cargo fell by 68,423 to 1,113,274 TEUs, which is yellow and 6,726 TEUs below target. Cruise throughput also declined by 227,701 to 5,109,379 guests, but it remained comfortably green. Berth and terminal utilization edged up another 0.2 percentage points to 84.8%, and petroleum throughput improved by 31,251 to 129,601,367 barrels while still missing the 130,000,000 target. This is still a managed yellow, not a break in the gateway strategy, but the signal is clear: congestion is starting to tax cargo reliability.
periods.recommendations: Treat March and April as a cargo recovery window: assign the Mobile Crane 3 crew to the Southport overflow string and clear reefers on Route C before 0700 each weekday. Keep the green cruise performance by maintaining the split-boarding playbook at Terminals 21 and 25, but do not let cruise labor pulls strip container yard coverage. My watch item is berth utilization above 84%; if it persists for three consecutive weeks, move two discretionary container calls to off-peak arrival windows with tariff incentives.

periods.analysis: Q2 showed the first clean correction in the arc: containerized cargo rose by 13,145 to 1,126,419 TEUs and returned to green. Cruise passengers declined seasonally by 924,579 to 4,184,800 guests, still above target, and that seasonal breathing room helped berth and terminal utilization drop by 3.6 percentage points to 81.2%. Petroleum throughput rebounded sharply by 4,219,661 to 133,821,028 barrels, back to green and above the 130,000,000 target. We are not home at 81.2%, but the operating system responded when we gave it cleaner windows and better yard discipline.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the TEU recovery by making the off-peak gate incentive permanent for at least one more quarter and adding a Saturday empty-return block for the Dole, Crowley, and Maersk pools. Use the lighter cruise shoulder season to finish pavement patching on the Terminal 19 coach loop and keep passenger turns green before the winter ramp-up. Continue the petroleum nomination calls every Monday morning, and keep the utilization watch focused on any week where Berths 7 through 10 exceed 83% combined occupancy.

periods.analysis: The gateway accelerated again in Q3: containerized cargo increased by 109,134 to 1,235,553 TEUs, the strongest point in this series so far. Cruise throughput also rose by 311,599 to 4,496,399 guests, and petroleum throughput eased by 1,058,765 to 132,762,263 barrels while remaining green. The price of that strength was familiar: berth and terminal utilization climbed by 1.7 percentage points to 82.9%, still yellow against the 80% ceiling. I like the demand profile, but I do not like needing perfect vessel sequencing to make the week work.
periods.recommendations: Lock in the green cargo result by extending the PierPass-style appointment compliance checks at Gates 3, 4, and 14 and publishing carrier scorecards for missed pickup windows. Keep cruise green by pre-staging buses on Eisenhower Boulevard for the two-ship Saturdays instead of stacking them inside the terminal loop. For the yellow berth condition, add one relief gang on high-density container days and test a 15-minute pilot dispatch interval for the Port Everglades turn basin during the September peak.

periods.analysis: Q4 repeated the pattern we cannot ignore: cruise surged by 913,334 to 5,409,733 guests, while containerized cargo decreased by 29,583 to 1,205,970 TEUs and stayed green. Berth and terminal utilization rose by 1.3 percentage points to 84.2%, putting us back near the pressure level we saw one year ago. Petroleum throughput dropped by 3,479,487 to 129,282,776 barrels, yellow and 717,224 barrels below target. The gateway is winning business, but winter cruise peaks and fuel variability are again exposing the same capacity seam.
periods.recommendations: Preserve the green cruise performance by keeping the four-lane debarkation model at Terminal 25 and adding contract wayfinding staff on the three highest guest-volume Sundays. For petroleum, require shipper-level recovery plans from the two customers behind the missed nominations and hold a mid-quarter dock-window review with the pipeline, terminal, and tug operators. To attack the recurring berth yellow, move the Harborview Port Community System berth board from daily updates to live updates for agents, pilots, CBP, and terminal operators by the next cruise peak.

periods.analysis: Q1 2026 was steadier but still too tight: containerized cargo declined by 84,979 to 1,120,991 TEUs, green by only 991 TEUs. Cruise throughput fell by 254,129 to 5,155,604 guests and remained a clear green, proving the winter product is durable. Berth and terminal utilization improved by 1.0 percentage point to 83.2%, but that is still above the 80% ceiling. Petroleum throughput increased by 132,008 to 129,414,784 barrels, which narrows the gap but remains yellow and 585,216 barrels short.
periods.recommendations: Do not coast on the narrow TEU green; assign a cargo-retention sprint to the Asia-Caribbean service lane and contact the top 20 beneficial cargo owners before the May contract cycle. Sustain cruise strength by renewing the luggage-valet vendor option for peak turn days and keeping CBP overtime pre-approved for double-ship mornings. My watch items are the 991-TEU cushion and 83.2% utilization; if either slips in the April forecast, activate the off-peak tariff discount and the overflow chassis lot at Eller Drive.

periods.analysis: Q2 gave us the best operating answer in a year: containerized cargo increased by 33,234 to 1,154,225 TEUs, safely green again. Cruise throughput declined seasonally by 883,917 to 4,271,687 guests, still green, and that helped berth and terminal utilization fall by 2.0 percentage points to 81.2%. Petroleum throughput jumped by 6,116,731 to 135,531,515 barrels, the strongest petroleum result in this sequence. We remain yellow because 81.2% is still above the 80% ceiling, but the arc is moving in the right direction: growth is being handled with more discipline, not just more overtime.
periods.recommendations: Make the Q2 playbook the standard: keep live berth-board discipline, retain the Saturday empty-return block, and extend the off-peak truck appointments through the next cargo peak. Protect the green petroleum result by reserving the current tanker-window cadence and auditing demurrage causes at Dock P-2 and Dock P-4. The next management target is simple and measurable: cut berth and terminal utilization from 81.2% to 80% or lower without giving back TEUs, guests, or barrels.

periods.analysis: Containers, cruise passengers and rolling petroleum throughput remain above their targets. Berth and terminal utilization nevertheless rose to 83.4%, above the 80% ceiling. Current trade growth and the capacity constraint need to appear side by side on the dashboard.
periods.recommendations: Keep the berth conflict calendar and truck appointment controls in force, and resolve overdue cargo-gate milestones before relying on automation for additional capacity.
